The opening line of The Canterbury Tales, written by Geoffrey Chaucer in Middle English during the late 14th century, is "Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote" which translates to modern English as "When April with its sweet showers." This line begins the General Prologue, setting the scene for the entire collection of tales.

The line is part of a longer passage that describes the coming of spring, when nature awakens from winter's dormancy and pilgrims begin their journeys to various holy sites. Chaucer composed this work while serving as a civil servant in London, drawing inspiration from Italian literature, particularly Boccaccio's Decameron. The Canterbury Tales was one of the first major works to be printed by William Caxton in 1478, who established his printing press in Westminster Abbey under the patronage of King Edward III. The original manuscript was written on parchment using a unique blend of oak gall ink and crushed lapis lazuli, giving it a distinctive bluish tint that was characteristic of royal documents of the period.

The opening line of Geoffrey Chaucer's "The Canterbury Tales," written in Middle English in the late 14th century, is "Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote." This famous line translates to modern English as "When April with its sweet showers."

This opening begins the General Prologue, which sets the scene for the entire collection of tales. The line is part of a longer passage describing the arrival of spring, which awakens nature from its winter slumber and inspires people to go on pilgrimages. Chaucer wrote this masterpiece between 1387 and 1394, drawing inspiration from other medieval works like Boccaccio's Decameron.

The manuscript was first printed by William Caxton in 1476, making it one of the earliest printed books in English history. The original manuscript was handwritten in a beautiful Gothic script, typical of medieval monasteries in southern England, and was preserved in Westminster Abbey until the early 1600s. The text gained widespread popularity among the emerging middle class, who found the stories particularly relatable to their daily lives in London's merchant districts.
